extracted.intended_audience: federal firearms licensees (FFLs), regulated firearms industry members, legal counsel, and public commenters on ATF rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Proposed ATF regulatory revisions to the definition of "engaged in the business" (dealer), related definitional provisions (personal collection, former licensee inventory, predominantly earn a profit), and supporting regulatory-review analyses for notice-and-comment rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory test for 'engaged in the business' (dealer)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A person who devotes time, attention, and labor to dealing in firearms as a regular course of trade or business to predominantly earn a profit through the repetitive purchase and resale of firearms. The term does not include a person who makes occasional sales, exchanges, or purchases of firearms to enhance a personal collection or for a hobby, or who sells all or part of the person's personal collection of firearms.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the primary statutory definition ATF proposes to retain (moved into §478.11). It emphasizes the combination of regular/repetitive dealing and predominant intent to obtain pecuniary gain; it explicitly preserves the statutory exception for occasional sales to enhance or liquidate a personal collection or hobby. ATF frames regulatory changes to align the regulations to this statutory text and remove regulatory provisions that expanded beyond it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal collection (EIB's narrow definition and ATF's proposed change)
rubrics_metrics.description: EIB defined “personal collection” as “[p]ersonal firearms that a person accumulates for study, comparison, exhibition ... or for a hobby (e.g., noncommercial, recreational activities for personal enjoyment...).” EIB also excluded “firearms accumulated primarily for personal protection.” ATF proposes rescinding the EIB subsection that narrowly defined personal collection and instead retaining a narrower, licensee-focused definition labeled “licensee personal collection.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF views the EIB definitions as overly restrictive by excluding some lawful, private, noncommercial purposes (e.g., self-defense). ATF proposes removing subsection (1) of the EIB definition and keeping subsection (2) only as guidance for licensees (to distinguish personal firearms from business inventory). The change is intended to avoid over-narrowing the statutory exception and to reduce confusion about lawful personal acquisition and occasional resale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'predominantly earn a profit'
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed definition: “The intent underlying the sale or disposition of firearms is predominantly one of obtaining pecuniary gain, as opposed to other intents, such as improving or liquidating a personal firearms collection. However, proof of profit, including the intent to profit, is not required in cases in which the person engaged in the regular and repetitive purchase and disposition of firearms for criminal purposes or terrorism.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF would move and retain this definition (with minor readability edits) to §478.11. ATF also proposes removing an EIB sentence not found in statute that stated a person may have intent to profit even if no pecuniary gain is actually obtained. The definition is used to distinguish dealers from other regulated categories (gunsmiths, pawnbrokers, manufacturers) and to clarify when proof of profit is unnecessary in criminal/terrorism contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Former licensee inventory treatment (EIB rule) and proposed rescission
rubrics_metrics.description: EIB treated firearms purchased as part of a licensee's business inventory while licensed as retaining that classification indefinitely; former licensees were permitted to dispose of inventory only (1) within 30 days after discontinuance (or longer for Director-approved good cause), or (2) on an “occasional” basis thereafter only to a licensee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF proposes removing the EIB definition of “former licensee inventory” and the 30‑day/occasional-sales restrictions from §§478.57 and 478.78. ATF reasons the permanent restraint on post-license sales is arguably unlawful and that occasional later private sales would not constitute repetitive purchase/resale covered by the GCA. ATF also acknowledges legitimate concerns about “fire sales” and recordkeeping but points to statutory prohibitions on engaging in the business without a license as the proper enforcement tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auctioneer exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The term does not include an auctioneer who provides only auction services on commission to assist in liquidating firearms at an estate-type auction, as long as the auctioneer does not purchase the firearms or take possession of the firearms for sale or consignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF proposes retaining and moving this explicitly codified auctioneer exception into §478.11 because ATF has historically provided consistent guidance on which auction activity crosses into dealing. Retention aims to preserve clarity and avoid confusion for industry members wanting to know when auction activity constitutes engaging in the business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttable presumptions and fact-pattern guidance in §478.13(b)-(h)
rubrics_metrics.description: EIB included paragraphs listing: (b) that engaged-in-the-business is fact-specific; (c) specific fact-patterns creating presumptions that a person is engaged in the business; (d) definition of “predominantly earn a profit”; (e) list of conduct that does not support a presumption; (f) evidence to rebut a presumption; (g) clarification that lists are not exhaustive; and (h) clarification that presumptions do not apply to criminal proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF proposes rescinding §§478.13(b)-(h). ATF explains the rebuttable presumptions and itemized fact patterns added by EIB caused confusion and commenters feared they could be misapplied to shift burdens of proof; one court stated the presumptions risked requiring owners to prove innocence. Removing these regulatory presumptions is intended to avoid that risk and to better align regulations with statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory necessity: when rulemaking (vs guidance) is required
rubrics_metrics.description: ATF considered alternatives: (1) maintaining status quo (no action), (2) rulemaking (proposed alternative), and (3) issuing guidance. ATF concluded rulemaking is necessary because guidance cannot rescind or alter regulatory presumptions and would not remedy confusion created by regulatory language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rulemaking when changes must alter existing regulatory text or remove regulatory presumptions; guidance is insufficient to change regulations or remove language that may be misapplied. The agency weighed confusion, potential chilling effects, and statutory alignment in selecting rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 cost–benefit and regulatory design standards
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 12866 directs agencies to assess costs and benefits of regulatory alternatives and select approaches that maximize net benefits. EO 13563 emphasizes quantifying costs/benefits, reducing costs, harmonizing rules, and promoting public flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF treats this proposed rule as a significant regulatory action under EO 12866 and provides analysis to comply. The rule is framed as deregulatory (aligning with statute), yielding qualitative benefits (reduced confusion) and qualitative costs (possible de minimis public-safety risk) but no quantifiable monetized costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 14192 deregulatory-offset consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 14192 requires agencies, for certain significant regulatory actions that impose incremental costs, to identify at least ten existing regulations to repeal or revise to offset costs. ATF determined this proposed rule would not be an EO 14192 regulatory action because it would not impose total costs greater than zero (it would be deregulatory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a new significant regulatory action imposes costs > 0, the agency should identify offsetting repeals; if the action imposes costs <= 0 (deregulatory), the EO14192 offset requirement does not apply. ATF documents its EO14192 analysis accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 14294 criminal regulatory-offense requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 14294 requires agencies promulgating regulations with criminal regulatory offenses to describe the conduct subject to criminal enforcement, authorizing statutes, and the mens rea standard applicable to each element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF states this proposed rule would not create a criminal regulatory offense and is thus exempt from EO 14294 requirements. Agencies must make the EO14294 disclosures when criminal regulatory offenses are newly created or modified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) certification/analysis requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the RFA (5 U.S.C. 601-612), agencies must conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis unless the agency head certifies with factual basis that the rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF certifies the proposed deregulatory rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities because it removes or amends provisions that expanded the statutory definition and observed no increase in licensure attributable to the EIB rule. ATF nonetheless invites comments on potential effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfunded Mandates Reform Act threshold test
rubrics_metrics.description: The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act requires agencies to assess whether a rule includes a federal mandate that would result in expenditures by state/local/tribal governments or the private sector of $100 million or more in any one year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ATF determined this proposed rule does not include such a mandate and thus no further actions under the Act are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) information-collection compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the PRA (44 U.S.C. 3501-3521), agencies must submit to OMB any information-collection requirements created or impacted by a rule and assess impacts on existing information collections. ATF identifies affected OMB control numbers (1140-0018, 1140-0019) and states the proposed changes would not add to or change respondent burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a rule affects information collections, the agency must prepare ICRs and coordinate with OMB; here ATF documents the relevant ICR numbers, summarizes Form 7/Form 8 purposes, and states no additional burden would result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federalism considerations (EO 13132)
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 13132 requires assessment of direct effects on states, the federal–state relationship, and distribution of power/responsibilities. ATF determined the proposed rule would not have substantial direct effects on states or preempt state law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must determine whether a rule warrants a federalism summary impact statement; ATF's determination avoids that requirement for this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of qualitative disbenefits (public-safety risk) vs. quantifiable costs
rubrics_metrics.description: ATF acknowledges potential qualitative disbenefits: rescinding parts of EIB may allow some active sellers who refrained to resume sales without licensing, possibly increasing risk to public safety. These risks are considered qualitative and speculative with no quantifiable monetized costs identified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory review should weigh both quantifiable and qualitative effects. ATF judges the public-safety risk de minimis relative to the goal of reducing confusion and perceived over-enforcement; agencies should document such qualitative considerations even when not monetizable.
